---
title: "Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations"
description: "Identifying what you do not know, recording it, and saying so honestly."
---

*Phases 2 and 3, design and analysis. [Where this sits in the
lifecycle](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).*

All analysis is uncertain. The question is never whether uncertainty exists, but whether you have
identified it, managed it, and told the reader about it in a way they can act on.

## What uncertainty is

Uncertainty describes the difference between an estimate and the true value. It arises from
measurement and sampling error, how data was collected, missing data, under-reporting, the
assumptions you had to make, and the limits of the method itself.

**Direct uncertainty** is uncertainty about an estimate that can be measured or quantified, and
communicated in absolute terms: a standard error, a confidence or credible interval, statistical
significance.

**Indirect uncertainty** is uncertainty about the underlying quality of knowledge surrounding an
estimate. It is not directly measured but inferred from the analysis. It is usually communicated as
caveats, or summarised on a qualitative or ordered scale such as
[the GRADE scale](https://gdt.gradepro.org/app/handbook/handbook.html).

Most analysis has both. Reporting only the first, because it is the one with a number attached, is a
common and misleading omission.

## Manage it from the start, not at the end

Uncertainty should be addressed during the analytical cycle so that the analysis can be
proportionately designed and planned, and so that assumptions, options and scenarios can be
appropriately chosen.[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

That is a design activity. By the time you are writing up, your options have narrowed to describing
the uncertainty you have. Handled at design, you can choose a method that reduces it.

The AQuA Book puts it more actively: at design you should **mine the planned analysis systematically
for possible sources and types of uncertainty**, so as to catch any large enough to breach the
acceptable margin of error.[^src-aqua-book-section-7-4] Mining is the right word. Uncertainty that is
waited for rather than hunted tends to surface after the result has been used.

You should:[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

- **identify the sources** of uncertainty and consider their impacts
- **analyse it at the level the decision requires**, and no further
- **develop options for managing it**, and take appropriate control and mitigation actions

## Assumptions

An assumption is something you have taken to be true without establishing it. Every analysis has
them. The failure is not making assumptions, it is leaving them unrecorded.

For each material assumption, record:

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| The assumption | Stated plainly, so someone else can judge it |
| Rationale | Why it is reasonable |
| Impact if wrong | Direction and rough scale. This is the field people skip and the one that matters |
| Sensitivity tested | Yes or no. At Level 3, tested where material |
| Agreed with | Who accepted it, and when |

The "impact if wrong" field is what turns a list of assumptions into something a commissioner can
use. An assumption whose failure would not change the conclusion is worth recording briefly. One
whose failure would reverse the conclusion needs stating in the output itself.

Where you can, **test the sensitivity of your key assumptions**, and plan that testing at design
stage rather than retrofitting it. The acceptable margin of error is agreed at scoping, along with
the levels of quality and certainty the analysis needs.[^src-govs-010-section-5-2] Sensitivity testing
is how you find out whether an assumption could push you past it. At Level 3 Comprehensive this is
required.
See [section 6](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd).

## Limitations

A limitation is something your analysis cannot do. State them in terms of use, not in terms of
method, because use is what the reader is deciding about.

Rather than "the data has incomplete coverage for two months", write "these figures understate
activity in July and August, so they should not be used to compare quarters".

The most useful sentence in any limitations section is usually: **"this analysis should not be used
to..."**, followed by the specific misuse it cannot support.

## Communicating it

When disseminating results, expressions of uncertainty should:[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

- **be quantitative where possible**
- be balanced, avoiding unwarranted confidence in a particular option

In practice:

- **Be transparent** about uncertainty, to avoid misinterpretation and misuse
- **Be specific** about what exactly is uncertain and why, how it has been quantified, the
  limitations of the data, and the assumptions made
- **Use plain language**, so that what you write about uncertainty can be understood by everyone who
  will read it
- **Show it in your visualisations**, data tables and datasets, and explain what it represents. It is
  not enough to confine it to a quality and methodology annex

::: {.callout-important title="Uncertainty is not a hedge" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Presented well, a range tells the commissioner whether the analysis is decisive. If the decision
would be the same at both ends of the plausible range, say so, and they can proceed with confidence.
If it would differ, that is often the most useful finding you have, and it may be worth reducing the
uncertainty before deciding rather than proceeding on the central estimate.

Quantified uncertainty makes analysis more useful, not less.
:::

For official statistics, Standard 7 of the Code of Practice requires producers to prominently
explain quality, including strengths and limitations, and to communicate the uncertainty in
estimates. See [section 2](../02-standards-landscape/index.qmd).
